::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Understanding limits and exact solutions](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4745296/understanding-limits-and-exact-solutions), asked by [Anon](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1205460/anon) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-07-31; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Consider the following equation:
>
> $\left(x^{2}-1\right)y=1-x$
>
> Setting $y{=}0$ forces the LHS equal to zero, so $x$ must be 1 for the RHS to be zero too. However, if we now rearrange the equation as,
>
> $y=\frac{1-x}{x^2 - 1}$,
>
> and we apply L'Hopital's rule, we see that when $x{=}1$, $y{=}{-}1/2$. We see also, that y is never equal to zero. So which is it? This seems contradictory to me. Please try to be thorough with your answer for me to understand.
:::

There's no need to bring calculus into this purely algebraic question.

Dividing both sides of an equation by an expression is only valid when that expression is nonzero. So your rearrangement loses one of the solutions.

I suggest setting one side of the equation to zero and factoring:
$$(x^2-1)y = 1-x \iff (x-1)(xy + y + 1) = 0$$
To satisfy this equation, one of the factors must be zero. If $x=1$, the equation is satisfied for any $y$ (including $y=0$). The second factor is zero if $y = - \frac{1}{x+1}$, which works as long as $x \neq -1$. The solution set is plotted below.
